common_name: Warm Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Orange-Bronze Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Warm Igloo is part of the patented Igloo series of naturally mounding, no-pinch hardy garden mums.

directions: Warm Igloo builds a dense, evenly rounded mound that disappears under double orange-bronze flowers deepening toward a darker bronze center as the display matures through fall. Like its Igloo-series siblings it needs no pinching to stay compact, breaking bud reliably in its first season without a prior summer of growth. Grow in full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the mound vigorous.

common_name: Autumn Spice Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Copper-Orange Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall into well-drained soil; this Igloo-series mum forms its dome shape without pinching.

directions: Autumn Spice Igloo covers its tidy, uniform cushion in double orange flowers washed with coppery-bronze overtones, giving a warmer, smokier look than the cleaner orange of its Pumpkin Igloo relative. The dense habit forms automatically through the growing season, so no pinching is required to keep plants compact and floriferous by late summer. Site in full sun with average, well-drained soil and consistent moisture while the root system establishes.

common_name: Firedance Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Ember-Orange Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Firedance Igloo (US Plant Patent 29,835) keeps its rounded cushion shape without pinching.

directions: Firedance Igloo produces single, daisy-type flowers in a hot, saturated red-orange highlighted by a golden center disc, reading as a steady sweep of ember color rather than fading dull as the season cools. The plant builds a dense, rounded mound through summer before breaking fully into bloom as days shorten in fall. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps in spring to maintain a tight habit.

common_name: Fireworks Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Lavender-Pink Quill-Petal Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; this Igloo-series mum needs no pinching to form its compact dome.

directions: Fireworks Igloo stands apart from its Igloo-series siblings with double, inch-wide flowers built of slender, tightly rolled quill-type florets in lavender-pink, fanning out from a bright yellow-orange center. Bloom color intensifies rather than fades as fall nights cool, giving the dense cushion a vivid, long-lasting display. Plant in full sun and well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and divide crowded mounds every few years to keep the habit tidy.

common_name: Snowy Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Double White Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall into well-drained soil; Snowy Igloo (US Plant Patent 26,998) forms its dome shape without pinching.

directions: Snowy Igloo opens from buttery-yellow buds into double white daisy flowers with soft creamy-white centers, held in dense clusters over dark green, finely cut foliage. The rounded, mounding habit develops uniformly without pinching, making it a reliable clean-white counterpart to the series' brighter colors for fall borders and mixed containers. Grow in full sun with average, well-drained soil, dividing the clump every few years to renew vigor.

common_name: Sundance Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Golden-Yellow Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Sundance Igloo keeps its mounded shape without pinching.

directions: Sundance Igloo covers its compact, rounded mound in clear, deep-gold daisy flowers that hold their saturated color through cool fall weather rather than fading. The uniform dome habit forms reliably in the plant's first season, giving a dependable, low-maintenance block of gold for borders and containers from late summer into October. Plant in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps in spring.

common_name: Dainty Pink Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Soft Pink Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall into well-drained soil; this Igloo-series mum forms a dome without pinching.

directions: Dainty Pink Igloo opens into a full cover of clear, light pink daisy flowers with cheerful yellow centers, staying soft and consistent in tone rather than muddying as nights turn cold. The naturally dense, dome-shaped habit requires no pinching, making it a dependable pastel option among the generally brighter Igloo-series colors. Grow in full sun in moderately fertile, well-drained soil, dividing the clump every two to three years.

common_name: Harvest Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Copper-Orange Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Harvest Igloo (US Plant Patent 29,152) forms its mounded shape without pinching.

directions: Harvest Igloo is covered in orange daisy flowers overlaid with coppery-bronze tones from early into late fall, giving a warmer, more muted finish than the series' clear orange cultivars. It forms a tidy, low mound of dark green, ferny foliage that stays attractive through the growing season and needs little more than an early-spring cleanup once flowering ends. Plant in full sun with average, well-drained soil; deer tend to leave it alone in favor of other garden plants.

common_name: Sunny Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Bright Yellow Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall into well-drained soil; Sunny Igloo forms its dome shape without pinching.

directions: Sunny Igloo bears bright double blossoms in sunshine yellow with caramel-gold centers, smothering the compact, rounded mound from late summer until the first hard frosts. Abundant, long-lasting flowering and a naturally tidy habit make it well suited to beds, borders, and pots without any pinching or staking. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, dividing established clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Brilliant Igloo Chrysanthemum (Hardy Sunny Yellow Cushion Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; Brilliant Igloo keeps its ball-shaped habit without pinching.

directions: Despite its fiery-sounding name, Brilliant Igloo produces masses of sunny yellow decorative flowers under two inches wide over a medium-sized, ball-shaped mound of green foliage. It flowers heavily and reliably in its first season without pinching, making it a dependable mid-size companion to the series' pink and red cultivars. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil, dividing the clump every two to three years to maintain a tight form.

common_name: Harry Anderton Chrysanthemum (Blush-Pink Anemone-Form Heirloom Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Harry Anderton is an heirloom anemone-type mum grown by cut-flower farms for its distinctive two-toned blooms.

directions: Harry Anderton is an heirloom anemone-form chrysanthemum bearing soft blush-pink ray florets surrounding a fuzzy, domed center dusted with gold, carried in generous sprays along each stem. It is a vigorous, floriferous grower favored by specialty cut-flower farms for its long vase life and resistance to shattering. Pinch young plants to encourage branching for spray production, and cut stems when flowers are roughly a quarter open for the longest-lasting arrangements; adding floral preservative and a touch of bleach to the vase water helps control the discoloration common to chrysanthemums.

common_name: Raymond Mounsey Chrysanthemum (Red Anemone-Centred Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Raymond Mounsey is classified as an anemone-centred (6a) exhibition type.

directions: Raymond Mounsey is a red anemone-centred chrysanthemum officially recognized in national cultivar classification registers under the anemone (6a) class, in which a raised, dome-like disc of short tubular florets is surrounded by a single ring of longer flat ray florets. Grow it as a disbudded single or spray stem depending on the finished bloom size wanted, staking early since exhibition-trained stems carry a heavy flower head. Propagate fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each late winter rather than dividing old clumps, which tend to produce smaller, less uniform blooms over time.

common_name: Seaton's Ruby Chrysanthemum (Red Anemone-Form Mum with Gold Reverse)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil; this anemone-type mum needs staking as it grows.

directions: Seaton's Ruby is an anemone-form chrysanthemum with broad red ray florets backed by a contrasting gold reverse, surrounding a raised central cushion of matching red disc florets. Its upright growth needs staking to support the flower heads, and because it is not reliably winter-hardy outside the warmest zones, gardeners in colder regions grow it from rooted cuttings replanted each spring. Flowering runs from September into October, and the blooms attract butterflies while holding up well in beds, borders, and cutting gardens with regular feeding through the season.

common_name: Klamath Falls Chrysanthemum (Yellow Anemone-Form Mum with Orange Center)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings as early in the season as possible in full sun and well-drained soil so the root system is well established before flowering begins.

directions: Klamath Falls produces small, bright yellow anemone-style flowers with a distinctive orange center disc, held over a mounded, bedding-friendly habit rather than the tall disbudded stems of show-type exhibition mums. It blooms heavily from September into October, extending color into the garden just as many other perennials are fading, and its flowers draw both birds and butterflies. It is not reliably winter-hardy outside its rated range, so plant it as early as conditions allow to maximize root establishment before the fall flush.

common_name: Westland Chrysanthemum (Pink Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, staking stems early to support the heavy spidery bloom.

directions: Westland is a quill-type exhibition chrysanthemum (US Plant Patent 4,589) bred at De Lier, Holland, from a cross of 'Yellow Augusta' and 'Dark Flamenco' and registered in 1973, distinguished by narrow, hollow, pink ray florets that curl slightly like tightly rolled quills around a reddish disc, giving the bloom an airy, spidery silhouette. The bud opens slowly, carried on strong, upright peduncles that hold the finished flower well clear of the foliage. Grow it as a disbudded single stem for the largest bloom, propagating fresh cuttings each year from overwintered stock rather than relying on an aging clump.

common_name: Belgian Mums Conella Yellow Chrysanthemum (Vivid Yellow Ball-Form Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants as early as possible in the season in full sun and well-drained soil to allow strong root establishment before flowering and winter; water thoroughly since the dense foliage can shed overhead irrigation before it reaches the soil.

directions: Conella Yellow (US Plant Patent 24,200) is part of the Belgian Mums line bred by the Belgian firm Gediflora for uniform, densely rounded, ball-shaped flowering habit, producing a prolific cover of vivid yellow blooms in mid-September across much of the Midwest and East. Plants form a tight, mounding shape prized for porch containers and front-of-border mass plantings. Because most garden mums perform better as dependable cold-tolerant annuals than as long-lived perennials, gardeners in colder zones should plant early in the season to give roots the best chance of carrying the clump through winter.

common_name: Belgian Mums Jasoda Purple Chrysanthemum (Deep Purple Ball-Form Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants early in the season in full sun and well-drained soil; Jasoda Purple blooms mid-to-late season, around early October across the Midwest and East.

directions: Jasoda Purple is one of the Gediflora-bred Belgian Mums, producing deep purple, rounded flowers in a lovely globe shape over a compact, mounding plant. Bloom arrives later in the season than many garden mums, making it a useful color for extending fall interest once earlier cultivars have faded. Grow in full sun and well-draining soil, watering thoroughly since the dense flower-covered foliage can deflect overhead watering away from the root zone, especially in containers.

common_name: Belgian Mums Jasoda Orange Chrysanthemum (Dark Orange Ball-Form Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants early in the season in full sun and well-drained soil; Jasoda Orange blooms mid-to-late season, around early October across the Midwest and East.

directions: Jasoda Orange, another of the Gediflora Belgian Mums, carries gorgeous dark orange flowers over a dense, nicely rounded ball-shaped habit that makes a strong late-season color statement. Like its Jasoda Purple counterpart, it flowers later than many garden mums, filling out the autumn display as other cultivars decline. Establish plants as early as possible in the growing season in full sun and well-drained soil, since perennializing success in cold climates depends on strong root development before winter.

common_name: Belgian Mums Aluga White Chrysanthemum (Clean White Ball-Form Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants as early as possible in the season in full sun and well-drained soil to establish roots before fall flowering and winter.

directions: Aluga White rounds out the Gediflora Belgian Mums line with clean white, densely double flowers over the same uniform, rounded habit shared by the series. Like its yellow, orange, and purple siblings, it is bred for even flowering and reliable garden performance rather than the disbudded single-stem culture used for exhibition mums. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and water deeply, since the thick blanket of foliage and flowers can shed light overhead watering before it reaches the root zone.

common_name: Daub's Frosted Juniper (Two-Toned Gold-Tipped Spreading Juniper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun, giving room for the almost ground-hugging spread.

directions: Daub's Frosted is a low, spreading juniper whose soft new growth emerges a frosted gold before maturing to blue-green, giving established plants a two-toned, speckled look rather than a solid color. Its almost ground-hugging habit makes an effective, textured groundcover on hot, dry banks and slopes where little else will thrive. It tolerates poor, shallow, or rocky soil, drought, and urban conditions once established, needing only full sun and well-drained ground to perform.

common_name: Mother Lode Juniper (Golden Low-Mounding Creeping Juniper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained, dryish or sandy soil in full sun, leaving ample room for the far-spreading mat to develop.

directions: Mother Lode (US Plant Patent 5,948) is a sport of the blue creeping juniper 'Wiltonii', forming an extremely low, feathery mat of bright gold summer foliage that deepens to a bronze-and-plum tone over winter. Branches root down as they spread, slowly building an irregular groundcover useful for draping over stone walls or weaving through other low conifers. It tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and air pollution once established, but resents consistently wet ground, so plant in full sun with sharp drainage.

common_name: Plumosa Juniperoides Sawara Cypress (Globular Dwarf Golden Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun for the best gold foliage color.

directions: This dwarf Sawara cypress starts out globe-shaped and becomes more conical with age, clothed in soft, stubby, awl-shaped foliage with a distinctive slight twist. New spring growth opens pale creamy-yellow, deepening to gold in summer before the oldest interior foliage gradually mellows toward light green. It is a slow grower best sited in full sun for strongest color, tolerating a range of well-drained soils and working well as a textured alternative to dwarf cedars in small gardens.

common_name: Nana Aurea Hinoki Cypress (Dwarf Golden Pyramidal Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, in a humid site for best color development.

directions: Nana Aurea is an old Japanese Hinoki cypress cultivar, first described in Western botanical literature by French botanist Elie-Abel Carriere in the mid-1860s, that builds a loose, irregular pyramid of dense golden-yellow foliage sprays mixed with cream and interior green. Reddish-brown bark shows through the branching for extra texture and contrast against the gold tips. It grows very slowly, making it a long-term fit for small gardens and large containers, and performs best with full sun to light shade and consistently moist, well-drained soil.

common_name: Sherwood Compact Mugo Pine (Dense Globose Dwarf Mountain Pine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in dry to average, very well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Sherwood Compact is a dense, tight, globose selection of mugo pine discovered in the 1950s in Oregon by plantsman Andy Sherwood, prized for its uniform mounded shape that needs little corrective pruning. Short, stiff, slightly twisted medium-green needles clothe the compact branches, and white winter buds give the mound a frosted, radiant look in the cold months. It is adaptable to most well-drained soils regardless of type or pH, performs well in containers or rock gardens, and can live for 50 years or more under good conditions.

common_name: Aurea Jakobsen Norway Spruce (Narrow Golden Slow-Growing Spruce)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun for best needle color.

directions: Aurea Jakobsen is a slow-growing, narrowly pyramidal Norway spruce selected in the late 1970s by Danish nurseryman Arne Vagn Jakobsen of Glamsbjerg, Denmark, notable for semi-pendant branches whose needles hold a frosted golden color on their upper surfaces year-round rather than only on new growth. Its narrow profile and very slow annual growth keep it proportional to small gardens for many years, unlike the full-size species. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil; it is commonly listed alongside dwarf and miniature conifers in collector catalogs even though it eventually grows taller and narrower than true dwarf forms.

common_name: Soft Whitlow-Grass (Caucasian Cushion Draba)

planting.note: Plant small rooted rosettes in spring into a gritty scree or trough mix in full sun; this cushion draba resents winter wet far more than cold.

directions: Native to dry, rocky mountain crevices of the Caucasus at high elevation, Draba mollissima forms a very compact, flat-to-hemispherical cushion built from dozens of tiny, softly white-hairy rosettes packed tightly together. In late spring the whole cushion is freely studded with small, soft-yellow flowers held just above the foliage in short, head-like clusters. Grow it in a sharply drained scree bed, raised trough, or rock garden crevice with maximum air movement, since excess humidity and winter moisture around the dense hairy rosettes are far more likely to cause rot than low temperatures.

common_name: Swiss Rock Jasmine (Limestone Cliff Cushion Androsace)

planting.note: Plant rooted non-flowering rosette cuttings in spring into a tufa rock crevice or sharply drained scree/trough mix in full sun; this is one of the most demanding true alpine cushion plants in cultivation.

directions: Androsace helvetica forms extremely dense, hard cushions five to ten centimeters across, built of minute rosettes packed so tightly the surface resembles a solid mound rather than individual plants. Tiny, nearly stalkless white flowers with a yellow throat appear singly or in pairs per rosette, native to limestone cliff crevices and crests of the Alps, Dolomites, and Pyrenees above 1,500 meters. In cultivation it is usually propagated from non-flowering rosette cuttings rather than seed, and succeeds best in a vertical tufa crevice or sharply drained scree with maximum exposure to sun and air movement, since standing moisture around the crown is its chief enemy.

common_name: Touran Deep Red Mossy Saxifrage (Compact Red-Flowered Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring into gritty, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Syngenta Touran series was bred for uniform, heavy flowering in containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Touran Deep Red is a modern seed-propagated color in the Touran series of mossy saxifrage, selected for compact, uniform mounds and an unusually long, heavy bloom period. Rich deep red, yellow-centered flowers blanket the dense evergreen foliage mat in mid-spring, giving a stronger, more saturated color than the older carmine-red Arends hybrids. Like other mossy saxifrages it needs cool, humus-rich, sharply drained soil and shade from hot afternoon sun, which scorches the fine moss-like foliage.

common_name: Touran Scarlet Mossy Saxifrage (Compact Scarlet-Flowered Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring into gritty, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Syngenta Touran series was bred for uniform, heavy flowering in containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Touran Scarlet is a bright, fiery-colored member of the seed-propagated Touran series of mossy saxifrage, forming the same tight, uniform evergreen mound as its series-mates but topped with vivid scarlet, yellow-centered flowers in mid-spring. The compact habit and even flowering make it reliable for mass plantings under high shade, where older, less uniform seed strains tend to bloom unevenly. Grow in cool, humus-rich, sharply drained soil with protection from hot afternoon sun to keep the fine foliage from browning.

common_name: Touran Neon Rose Mossy Saxifrage (Compact Bright Pink-Flowered Arends Rockfoil)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring into gritty, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the Syngenta Touran series was bred for uniform, heavy flowering in containers as well as garden beds.

directions: Touran Neon Rose rounds out the Touran series with vivid, bright pink, yellow-centered flowers held just above a dense, uniform mat of small evergreen rosettes. It shares the series' long, heavy mid-spring bloom period and compact, even habit, making it dependable for containers and shaded rock garden plantings where flowering consistency matters. Provide cool, humus-rich, sharply drained soil and afternoon shade, since the fine moss-like foliage browns quickly under hot direct sun.
